new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (p. 689 of Tryon ed. 1995, Comparative Austronesian Dictionary, chapter 43 "Dami" by George Elliott) and read it by eye: section 2.1 "Word stress" reads exactly "Stress falls on alternate syllables, the primary stress normally falling on the final syllable of a word. Primary stress may be attracted away from a final open non-nasalised single vowel syllable, if the vowel in a preceding syllable is lower in terms of tongue height than that of the final syllable, or if the nucleus of a preceding syllable contains a vowel sequence." Verbatim match with the reported quote and with the scanned file full-text source lines 58555-58775; the archive.org page map puts pp. 687-690 at leaves 733-…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Default primary stress on the final syllable, with an alternating (every-other-syllable) rhythm running leftwards from it. Primary stress is pulled off a final syllable that is light (open, single oral vowel) onto a preceding syllable whose vowel is lower (more sonorous) than the final vowel or whose nucleus is a vowel sequence (heavy). Closed finals, nasalised-vowel finals and finals with vowel sequences keep final stress. Classified weight-sensitive because the retraction is governed by nucleus weight (vowel sequences) and vowel height, not by lexical marking; a reviewer could equally file it as fixed: final syllable with weight/sonority-driven retraction.
new_statements.secondary_stress: "Stress falls on alternate syllables" - secondary stresses on every other syllable counted from the primary (normally final) stress; direction and count not spelled out further.
new_statements.exceptions: Only the phonological retraction conditions quoted (final open non-nasalised single-vowel syllable vs. lower vowel or vowel sequence in a preceding syllable); no lexical exceptions listed; the hedges "normally" and "may be" are the author's.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level ("final syllable of a word"); Southern dialect; the description is a brief overview in a wordlist introduction, with the author pointing to unpublished SIL Ukarumpa papers (Elliott n.d. "Dami phonology") for detail.
new_statements.identity_note: The source describes the Southern (Gonoa-Kuyombon) dialect of Dami explicitly ("Below is a brief overview of the phonology of Dami (Southern dialect)", p. 689); Elliott also says pronunciation varies very little between the Southern, Western (Barum-Mair-Atu) and Northern (Derin-Tadub-Bur) dialects (p. 688). Glottolog lists no dialect-level glottocodes under mari1428, so the statement is taken to hold for the language as a whole. Dami = Ham = Marik (ISO dad); Ross 1988 lists it as "Ham (= Dami)".

sources.note: Section 2.1 Word stress, p. 689: alternating stress, primary normally final; primary retracted from a final open non-nasalised single-vowel syllable to a preceding syllable with a lower vowel or a vowel sequence. scanned taken from the archive.org full text already. page images pp. 687/689/690 downloaded now from the open archive.org item and the p. 689 image checked by eye - quote verbatim.

Alternate names Dami, Ham, Marik; only descriptive references are Elliott 1995 and Elliot 1979; Ross 1988 pp. 160-173 cited for subclassification. The held Glottolog 5.1 sources.bib has ~20 further [dad] entries, all Elliott, Wendy vernacular readers/Bible stories (1990-2000), none descriptive.
Coded by J. A. Goodall and H. Skirgard from Elliot 1979 'Dami Grammar Essentials'; no stress features.
